lessons.title: Characteristics of Digestate: Nutrients and Organic Matter
lessons.body: Digestate is the leftover material after biogas production. It is a thick, dark slurry that smells less than raw manure but still contains valuable nutrients. On average, digestate from cattle manure has about 1.5-2.5% nitrogen (N), 0.8-1.5% phosphorus (P2O5), and 1.5-2.5% potassium (K2O) on a dry matter basis. The exact numbers depend on the feedstock. For example, digestate from pig manure is richer in nitrogen, while digestate from crop residues is lower. Unlike fresh manure, up to 80% of the nitrogen in digestate is in the ammonium form, which plants can use quickly. The organic matter content is 30-50% of dry matter, which improves soil structure and water holding capacity. In Africa, where many soils are sandy and low in organic matter, applying digestate can increase yields of maize, vegetables, and fodder by 20-50% compared to no fertilizer. However, digestate is not a complete fertilizer. It often lacks enough phosphorus for high-demand crops like potatoes. Also, if the feedstock includes animal bedding or food waste, the digestate may contain weed seeds or pathogens. Testing is key: a simple soil test kit or a lab analysis (costing $20-50) can tell you the exact N-P-K and pH. Without testing, you risk over-applying nitrogen, which can burn plants or leach into groundwater. Store digestate in a covered tank or lined pit to prevent nutrient loss from rain and sun. For small-scale farmers, a 200-liter drum with a lid works well. Use within 3-6 months for best nutrient availability.

lessons.title: Digestate Separation: Solid and Liquid Fractions
lessons.body: Fresh digestate is a thick slurry, often 5-10% dry matter. To make it easier to handle and use, separate it into solid and liquid fractions. The solid fraction is like a moist compost, while the liquid fraction is a thin, nutrient-rich tea. You can separate manually or with a machine. For small farms (1-5 cows), a simple screen or a screw press made from a modified grain auger works. A basic screw press costs $500-1500 and can process 1-2 cubic meters per hour. For larger farms, a decanter centrifuge ($10,000-30,000) separates more efficiently, but it needs electricity. Manual separation: pour digestate through a 5-mm mesh screen. The solids stay on top; the liquid drains into a container. The solid fraction contains more organic matter and phosphorus (2-3% N, 1-2% P2O5, 1-2% K2O on dry basis), while the liquid fraction is rich in ammonium nitrogen (0.1-0.3% N) and potassium. Use the solid fraction as a soil amendment or compost it further. The liquid fraction is ideal for fertigationâmixing with irrigation water. In Kenya, farmers using separated digestate liquid on kale (sukuma wiki) reported 30% higher yields than those using raw manure. Separation also reduces transport costs: liquid can be pumped through pipes or carried in jerrycans, while solids are easier to stack and store. Store liquid in a covered tank to prevent nitrogen loss; store solids under a tarp to keep them dry. Always wear gloves and boots when handling, as the liquid can contain harmful bacteria. After separation, clean equipment with water to prevent corrosion.

lessons.title: Composting and Drying of Solid Digestate
lessons.body: Solid digestate from separation is still wet and may contain weed seeds or pathogens. Composting and drying turn it into a stable, safe, and easy-to-use fertilizer. Composting: mix solid digestate with dry carbon materials like maize stalks, rice husks, or sawdust in a 1:1 ratio by volume. Aim for a moisture content of 50-60% (squeeze test: a handful should feel like a wrung-out sponge). Build a pile 1-1.5 meters high and 2 meters wide. Turn the pile every 3-4 days for the first two weeks, then weekly. The pile should heat up to 55-65Â°C within 2-3 days, which kills most pathogens and weed seeds. After 4-6 weeks, the compost is dark, crumbly, and smells earthy. In Uganda, farmers composting digestate with coffee husks produced a compost with 2.5% nitrogen, 1.5% phosphorus, and 2% potassiumâbetter than many commercial organic fertilizers. Drying: spread solid digestate in thin layers (5-10 cm) on a concrete slab or black plastic sheet in full sun. Turn it daily. In dry season, it takes 3-5 days to dry to 15-20% moisture. In wet season, use a solar dryer or a covered shed with ventilation. Dried digestate can be stored in sacks for 6-12 months. You can also pelletize dried digestate using a simple pellet mill ($800-2000) to make it easier to apply and sell. Pellets are popular for urban gardening. Always test compost and dried digestate for nutrient content before applying, as nutrient levels vary. Apply compost at 2-5 tonnes per hectare for cereals, or 1-2 kg per square meter in vegetable gardens.

lessons.title: Using Digestate as Biofertilizer: Application Rates and Timing
lessons.body: Digestate is a powerful biofertilizer, but you must apply it correctly to avoid burning crops or wasting nutrients. First, know your soil and crop needs. A soil test (available at local agricultural offices for $10-30) tells you existing nutrients. For maize in Africa, a typical recommendation is 100-150 kg nitrogen per hectare. If your digestate liquid has 0.2% nitrogen (2 g per liter), you need 50,000-75,000 liters per hectareâthat's 5-7.5 liters per square meter. That sounds like a lot, but you can split applications. Apply half at planting and half 4-6 weeks later when plants are actively growing. For vegetables like tomatoes, apply 2-3 liters of liquid digestate per plant every two weeks, diluted 1:1 with water to prevent leaf burn. Solid digestate or compost: apply 2-5 tonnes per hectare (200-500 g per square meter) before planting and mix into the top 15 cm of soil. Timing matters: apply liquid digestate in the cool of the morning or evening to reduce ammonia loss. Do not apply before heavy rain, as nutrients will wash away. For rain-fed crops, apply at the start of the rainy season. For irrigated crops, inject digestate into drip lines or add to furrows. In Ethiopia, farmers using digestate on wheat applied 4 tonnes per hectare of solid digestate plus 20,000 liters per hectare of liquid, yielding 30% more than those using only urea. Always wear gloves and avoid direct contact with skin. Store digestate away from water sources to prevent contamination. Keep records of application rates and crop yields to fine-tune your program each season.

lessons.title: Regulations and Safety Considerations for Digestate Use
lessons.body: Digestate is a valuable resource, but it can also carry risks. Regulations vary by country, but most African nations have basic rules for organic waste and fertilizer use. In Kenya, the Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) sets limits for heavy metals and pathogens in organic fertilizers. In South Africa, the Fertilizers, Farm Feeds, Agricultural Remedies and Stock Remedies Act (Act 36 of 1947) regulates digestate if sold. For on-farm use, you often don't need a license, but you must follow safety practices. First, pathogen control: digestate from biogas plants that treat manure at 35-55Â°C for at least 20 days reduces pathogens like E. coli and Salmonella, but some may survive. Composting solid digestate at 55Â°C for 3 days kills most pathogens. Never apply raw liquid digestate to crops eaten raw (e.g., lettuce, carrots) within 30 days of harvest. For root crops, wait 60 days. Second, heavy metals: if your feedstock includes industrial waste or batteries, digestate can contain lead, cadmium, or zinc. Test annually if you use such inputs. Third, ammonia emissions: liquid digestate can lose up to 50% of its nitrogen as ammonia if left uncovered. Cover storage tanks and incorporate liquid into soil within 4 hours of application. Fourth, water protection: keep digestate 30 meters away from wells, rivers, and streams. Use a lined storage pit or tank. Fifth, personal safety: wear gloves, boots, and eye protection when handling. Wash hands and clothes after use. In Rwanda, the Rwanda Environment Management Authority (REMA) requires biogas users to have a digestate management plan. Check with your local agricultural extension officer for specific rules in your area. Following these steps protects your health, your community, and your soil.

lessons.title: Case Study: Integrated Nutrient Management with Digestate
lessons.body: In central Malawi, the Mchinji Biogas Project installed 50 household biogas digesters for smallholder farmers. Each digester (6 cubic meters) processes manure from 2-3 cows. Before biogas, farmers used raw manure or expensive urea. After installation, they faced a new challenge: what to do with the digestate? The project introduced integrated nutrient management. Farmers separated digestate into solid and liquid. Solid was composted with maize cobs and applied to maize fields at 3 tonnes per hectare. Liquid was diluted 1:2 with water and applied to vegetables (tomatoes, onions, leafy greens) every two weeks. They also rotated crops: maize followed by beans to fix nitrogen. Results after two seasons: maize yields increased from 1.5 to 2.8 tonnes per hectare (87% increase). Vegetable yields doubled. Farmers saved $120 per season on urea. Soil organic matter rose from 0.8% to 1.4% in three years. The key was combining digestate with other practices: no burning of crop residues, minimal tillage, and use of cover crops. One farmer, Grace Banda, said: 'I used to buy fertilizer on credit. Now I use my cow's manure twiceâfirst for gas, then for crops.' Challenges included initial cost of separation screens ($50 each) and training on application rates. The project provided training and a shared screw press. Lessons learned: (1) Start smallâtest on one plot. (2) Test digestate and soil yearly. (3) Train all family members. (4) Keep records. (5) Share knowledge with neighbors. This case shows that digestate is not wasteâit's a resource that can transform African farms when used wisely.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Digestate Management and Utilization

Digestate is the residual material left after anaerobic digestion of organic feedstocks â and for African agribusinesses, it is not waste. It is a revenue stream, a fertiliser substitute, and a soil amendment that can cut input costs by 30â60% when managed correctly. This practical reference gives you the numbers, tables, and safety rules you need to turn digestate into profit.

Whether you run a 50-cow dairy, a municipal biodigester, or a commercial biogas plant supplying off-takers, the decisions below determine whether digestate becomes a cost centre or a business line.

Lesson 1: Characteristics of Digestate â Nutrients and Organic Matter

Digestate composition varies with feedstock, digester type, and retention time. Typical nutrient values for African contexts are shown below.

Table 1: Typical Nutrient Content of Digestate by Feedstock (per tonne fresh weight)
Feedstock Total N (kg) PâOâ (kg) KâO (kg) Organic Matter (%) Dry Matter (%)
Cattle slurry4.51.83.2658
Pig slurry6.02.54.0606
Poultry litter12.08.06.55525
Maize silage3.51.22.87510
Food waste8.03.04.55012

Source: Adapted from FAO (2019) and Teagasc (2020), Digestate as a Fertiliser.

Business implication: A 100-cow dairy producing 15 tonnes of slurry daily yields roughly 67 kg N, 27 kg PâOâ, and 48 kg KâO per day in digestate. At 2024 Kenyan fertiliser prices, that is over USD 90/day in nutrient value â before accounting for biogas revenue.

Lesson 2: Digestate Separation â Solid and Liquid Fractions

Separation concentrates nutrients. The solid fraction is rich in organic matter and phosphorus; the liquid fraction carries most of the nitrogen and potassium.

Table 2: Nutrient Partitioning After Mechanical Separation (% of total nutrient)
Fraction Total N PâOâ KâO Dry Matter Best Use
Solid fraction25â35%70â85%20â30%20â30%Compost, soil amendment
Liquid fraction65â75%15â30%70â80%2â6%Fertigation, foliar feed

Source: Adapted from Moller et al. (2000), Journal of Agricultural Engineering Research, and IRENA (2021).

Business implication: Separation enables two product lines â a bagged solid compost for horticulture and a liquid fertiliser for drip irrigation. In South Africa, separated liquid digestate sells for ZAR 1.50â3.00 per litre to vineyard and orchard operations.

Lesson 3: Composting and Drying of Solid Digestate

Raw solid digestate is not stable. Composting for 6â10 weeks reduces pathogens, stabilises carbon, and produces a marketable product. Drying (sun or forced-air) reduces moisture from 70% to 20%, cutting transport costs.

  • Composting: Windrow turning every 3â5 days. C:N ratio 25â30:1. Temperature 55â65Â°C for pathogen kill.
  • Drying: Solar tunnel dryers achieve 15â20% moisture in 5â7 days in East African conditions.
  • Value addition: Composted digestate can be blended with rock phosphate or biochar for premium organic fertiliser.

Lesson 4: Using Digestate as Biofertiliser â Application Rates and Timing

Apply digestate based on crop nitrogen requirement, not on volume. The table below gives practical rates for common African crops.

Table 3: Recommended Digestate Application Rates (liquid fraction, 0.3% N)
Crop N Requirement (kg/ha) Digestate Rate (mÂ³/ha) Timing
Maize (grain)12040Split: 50% at planting, 50% at V6
Tomato (field)1505030% at transplant, 70% fertigation
Kale (leafy)10033Split: 50% at 2 weeks, 50% at 6 weeks
Banana20067Quarterly splits
Tea18060Split: 3 applications per season

Source: Adapted from FAO (2019) and KALRO (2022), Organic Fertiliser Guidelines for Kenya.

Timing rules:

  • Apply to moist soil, early morning or late afternoon.
  • Incorporate liquid digestate within 4 hours to reduce ammonia loss.
  • Avoid application before heavy rain (runoff risk) or on waterlogged soils.
  • Do not apply to leafy vegetables within 30 days of harvest if not composted.
â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING:

Raw digestate may contain Salmonella, E. coli, Cryptosporidium, and heavy metals (Zn, Cu, Cd). Never apply raw digestate to crops eaten raw within 30 days of harvest. Wear gloves and boots during handling. In South Africa, digestate use is regulated under the Fertilizers, Farm Feeds, Agricultural Remedies and Stock Remedies Act (Act 36 of 1947). In Kenya, follow KEBS KS 2295:2017 for organic fertiliser safety. Test digestate for heavy metals annually.

Lesson 5: Regulations and Safety Considerations for Digestate Use

Regulations vary by country. Key compliance points for African agribusinesses:

  • Kenya: KEBS KS 2295:2017 â maximum heavy metal limits (Cd 3 mg/kg, Pb 100 mg/kg).
  • South Africa: Act 36 of 1947 â registration required for commercial fertiliser sales.
  • Nigeria: NAFDAC registration for packaged organic fertiliser.
  • Uganda: UNBS certification for organic inputs.
  • EU export markets: EU Regulation 2019/1009 â digestate must meet pathogen and contaminant limits.

Business tip: Get your digestate tested at a certified lab (e.g., SGS, Bureau Veritas) before selling. Certification opens premium markets and protects against liability.

Lesson 6: Case Study â Integrated Nutrient Management with Digestate

Case: BioBuu Ltd, Uganda (2023)

BioBuu operates a 200 mÂ³ biodigester processing 5 tonnes/day of market waste and cattle manure in Kampala. Before 2022, digestate was discharged to a lagoon. After separation and composting:

  • Solid compost: 1.2 tonnes/day sold at UGX 800/kg to horticulture farms â USD 260/day revenue.
  • Liquid fertiliser: 3 mÂ³/day sold at UGX 1,500/litre to urban vegetable growers â USD 120/day revenue.
  • Cost saving: Neighbouring maize farm replaced 50% of urea with liquid digestate, saving USD 45/ha/season.
  • Payback: Separation and composting equipment (USD 18,000) paid back in 14 months.

Lesson: Digestate is a product, not a by-product. Separation + composting + certification = three revenue streams from one waste stream.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Test digestate quarterly for N-P-K, dry matter, pH, and heavy metals.
  2. Separate solid and liquid fractions to maximise market value.
  3. Compost solid fraction for 6â10 weeks before sale or field use.
  4. Apply liquid digestate at rates matching crop N requirement â never exceed 250 kg N/ha/year.
  5. Incorporate within 4 hours to reduce ammonia loss and odour.
  6. Observe 30-day harvest interval for raw digestate on edible crops.
  7. Register your product with KEBS, NAFDAC, or Act 36 authority before commercial sale.
  8. Keep records of application rates, dates, and crop responses for 3 years.

Further Reading

  • FAO (2019) â The Role of Digestate in Sustainable Agriculture
  • IRENA (2021) â Renewable Energy and Agriculture in Africa
  • Teagasc (2020) â Digestate as a Fertiliser
  • KEBS KS 2295:2017 â Organic Fertiliser Specification (Kenya)
  • South Africa Act 36 of 1947 â Fertilizer Regulation

Prepared for RISE AFRICA Skills â Biogas Systems Module. Always verify local regulations with your national bureau of standards before commercialising digestate products.

quiz.q: What is the typical nitrogen content range of digestate from cattle manure?
quiz.explanation: Digestate from cattle manure typically contains 1.5-2.5% nitrogen on a dry matter basis.

quiz.q: Which fraction of digestate is richer in ammonium nitrogen?
quiz.explanation: The liquid fraction contains more ammonium nitrogen, which is readily available to plants.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool for separating digestate on a small farm?
quiz.explanation: A 5-mm mesh screen is a low-cost manual method for separating solid and liquid fractions.

quiz.q: What moisture content is ideal for composting solid digestate?
quiz.explanation: A moisture content of 50-60% supports microbial activity and heating during composting.

quiz.q: How long should compost be turned every 3-4 days to ensure pathogen kill?
quiz.explanation: Turning every 3-4 days for the first two weeks helps maintain high temperatures that kill pathogens.

quiz.q: What is the recommended application rate of liquid digestate for maize if it contains 0.2% nitrogen?
quiz.explanation: To supply 100-150 kg N per hectare, you need 50,000-75,000 liters of 0.2% N digestate.

quiz.q: When is the best time to apply liquid digestate to reduce ammonia loss?
quiz.explanation: Applying in cool conditions reduces volatilization of ammonia.

quiz.q: What is a safety consideration when using digestate on crops eaten raw?
options: B) Wait at least 30 days after application before harvest
quiz.explanation: A 30-day interval reduces the risk of pathogen contamination on raw-eaten crops.

quiz.q: Which organization regulates organic fertilizers in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: The Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) sets standards for organic fertilizers.

quiz.q: In the Malawi case study, what was the increase in maize yield after using digestate?
quiz.explanation: Maize yields increased from 1.5 to 2.8 tonnes per hectare, an 87% increase.

quiz.q: What is the primary form of nitrogen in digestate that plants can use quickly?
quiz.explanation: Up to 80% of nitrogen in digestate is in the ammonium form, which is readily available.

quiz.q: Which of these is a benefit of separating digestate?
quiz.explanation: Separation makes digestate easier to handle and apply, and reduces transport costs.

quiz.q: What temperature range should a compost pile reach to kill pathogens?
quiz.explanation: Temperatures of 55-65Â°C for several days kill most pathogens and weed seeds.

quiz.q: How long can dried digestate be stored in sacks?
quiz.explanation: Dried digestate can be stored for 6-12 months if kept dry.

quiz.q: What is a recommended application rate for solid digestate compost on cereals?
quiz.explanation: 2-5 tonnes per hectare is a typical rate for cereals like maize.

quiz.q: Which safety practice is recommended when handling digestate?
quiz.explanation: Wearing gloves and boots protects against pathogens and skin irritation.

quiz.q: What is the minimum distance digestate storage should be from water sources?
quiz.explanation: A 30-meter buffer prevents contamination of wells, rivers, and streams.

quiz.q: In the Malawi case study, what was the soil organic matter increase after three years?
quiz.explanation: Soil organic matter rose from 0.8% to 1.4% over three years.

quiz.q: What is a key lesson from the integrated nutrient management case study?
options: B) Start small and test on one plot
quiz.explanation: Starting small and testing allows farmers to learn and adjust without risk.

quiz.q: Which nutrient is often lacking in digestate for high-demand crops like potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Digestate often has insufficient phosphorus for phosphorus-demanding crops.

quiz.q: What is a simple test to check moisture content of compost?
quiz.explanation: The squeeze test: a handful should feel like a wrung-out sponge.

quiz.q: How often should you turn a compost pile after the first two weeks?
quiz.explanation: After the first two weeks of frequent turning, turn weekly until compost is ready.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of pelletizing dried digestate?
options: B) Makes it easier to apply and sell
quiz.explanation: Pellets are easier to handle, apply, and market, especially for urban gardening.

quiz.q: Which of these is a regulation for digestate use in South Africa?
quiz.explanation: The Fertilizers, Farm Feeds, Agricultural Remedies and Stock Remedies Act (Act 36 of 1947) regulates fertilizers.

quiz.q: What should you do if your digestate feedstock includes industrial waste?
options: B) Test for heavy metals annually
quiz.explanation: Industrial waste can introduce heavy metals, so annual testing is necessary.

quiz.q: How soon should liquid digestate be incorporated into soil after application?
quiz.explanation: Incorporating within 4 hours minimizes ammonia volatilization.

quiz.q: What is the recommended dilution for liquid digestate applied to tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: Diluting 1:1 with water helps prevent leaf burn on tomatoes.

quiz.q: What is a key challenge mentioned in the Malawi case study?
options: B) Initial cost of separation screens
quiz.explanation: The initial cost of separation screens ($50 each) was a challenge.

quiz.q: Which practice helps increase soil organic matter when using digestate?
quiz.explanation: Minimal tillage, along with digestate use, helps build soil organic matter.

quiz.q: What is the recommended waiting period before harvesting root crops after digestate application?
quiz.explanation: For root crops, a 60-day interval is recommended to reduce pathogen risk.
